subject: 🥵 Too hot for comfort
body_html:
Plus: Economic anecdata | Thursday, October 15, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Macro
By Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown · Oct 15, 2026

It's supposed to reach 91 degrees in Bangkok around the time Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh is scheduled to appear Friday (late this evening U.S. time) — but it's the U.S. economy that is running unmistakably hot. 🥵

  • Today, we look at how the latest inflation and retail sales readings add to Warsh's dilemma over whether to raise interest rates again late this month.
  • Plus, the latest Beige Book tells the same story, in anecdotal form. More below.

Today's newsletter, edited by Jeffrey Cane and copy edited by Amy Stern, is 912 words, a 3.5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: The too-hot-for-comfort economy
 
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Data this week has all told the same story: This is a rip-roaring U.S. economy with all the inflationary pressures that might imply.

The big picture: It puts Warsh and the Fed in a difficult jam. Top officials have signaled patience in further interest rate hikes in recent weeks, but the latest data implies broader inflationary pressures than previously thought, testing that conviction.

  • There is scant evidence that price pressures are receding on their own and growing reason to fear that they are becoming more entrenched, which could compel a more aggressive rate-hiking response.

Driving the news: Just this morning, the government said the Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September, the highest since 2022 and far above the 0.6% analysts expected. It came on the heels of a too-hot-for-comfort reading on consumer prices yesterday.

  • Also this morning, September retail sales notched a 0.8% rise, versus the 0.4% analysts had expected. And the August number was revised higher.
  • There were only 199,000 initial claims for unemployment benefits last week, remaining near historic lows.

Between the lines: The U.S. growth juggernaut shows no sign of diminishing — but neither do the price pressures that have bedeviled the economy for nearly five consecutive years.

  • If anything, the PPI and CPI data released this week suggest inflation is broadening, showing up in sectors well beyond energy.

State of play: In his appearance at the International Monetary Fund's meetings in Thailand Friday (11:30pm ET tonight), Warsh has a final opportunity to comment before the Fed enters its customary quiet period in advance of a policy meeting that concludes Oct. 28.

  • Colleagues including New York Fed president John Williams and vice chair Philip Jefferson gave rather clear signaling in the last couple of weeks that they see little urgency to raise rates at a second consecutive meeting this month.
  • Warsh faces a dilemma. If he affirms that stance in spite of the hot price data, it could raise doubts about his determination to bring inflation under control.
  • If he seems inclined to raise rates, he could seem overly reactive to a couple of economic releases, contrary to his stated goal of making the Fed less "data-point dependent."

The intrigue: Surprisingly, bond yields are down today despite the hot PPI number — and a surge in yields following the CPI number yesterday mostly reversed later in the trading session.

  • It seems to reflect a flight to quality among traders as optimism around the AI buildout fades. With semiconductor and related stocks down, money looks to be flowing into safer Treasury securities.
  • The policy-sensitive two-year Treasury yield briefly touched 4.95% after the CPI number yesterday, implying significant Fed rate hikes ahead. It's down to 4.72% this morning — an astonishing move for any 24-hour period, let alone one that included hotter-than-expected inflation data.

What they're saying: "Today's September PPI report reinforces yesterday's CPI message that inflation is turning higher and moving in the wrong direction for the Fed," Nationwide financial market economist Oren Klachkin wrote in a note.

  • "AI continues to lend upside pressure from categories directly and indirectly tied to the buildout. Businesses seem to be passing higher costs onto customers as the proxy for margins rose heftily in September."

2. Telling economic anecdotes
 

Illustration: Tiffany Herring/Axios
 

A grocery chain says it now costs more to ship a head of lettuce from California than to buy the lettuce itself. Tech companies are trying to purchase entire inventories of electrical equipment to build data centers.

Why it matters: These anecdotes from the Fed's latest Beige Book show how two extraordinary forces — the AI buildout and the Iran war — are changing decisions about spending, investment and hiring.

  • The implications extend beyond individual firms, with consequences for inflation and employment, as the Fed weighs another rate hike.

Zoom in: A grocery chain told the Richmond Fed that diesel prices have risen 30% from a year earlier — making shipping lettuce more expensive than the cost of the vegetable — but price-sensitive customers have left it unable to pass along the higher costs.

  • The energy shock is also squeezing businesses locked into earlier contracts: A Montana timber company said fuel costs had more than doubled on a project negotiated months earlier.

The AI boom is creating another strain, intensifying competition for equipment needed to build data centers.

  • An electrical equipment distributor told the Chicago Fed that tech companies tried to buy up all of its available equipment. Suppliers resisted, citing commitments to other customers.

What to watch: AI is changing how many workers businesses believe they need and what they need them to do in ways not yet apparent in broader labor market data.

  • In Dallas, an accounting industry contact said some large firms were delaying employment contracts because AI productivity gains could reduce their need for entry-level workers.
  • A staffing firm in the area said AI agents conducted more than 180 hours of job interviews in two days, leaving human recruiters to review the results and make hiring decisions.
